title: The Second Declension — Neuter
subtitle: templum, dōnum, bellum. Neuter nominative and accusative always identical.
objectives: Decline second-declension neuter nouns in all cases, both numbers.
Recognize that neuter nominative and accusative are always identical.
Apply the neuter plural rule: neuter plurals take plural verbs.
Translate sentences with neuter subjects and objects.

sections.heading: The second declension: neuter nouns
sections.body:
Neuter nouns of the second declension end in -um. They follow the same pattern as masculine nouns, with two exceptions:
  1. The nominative and accusative are always identical in both numbers.
  2. The nominative and accusative plural end in -a, not -ī or -ōs.

Paradigm:

          Singular    Plural
  Nom.    templum     templa
  Gen.    templī      templōrum
  Dat.    templō      templīs
  Acc.    templum     templa
  Abl.    templō      templīs

This pattern holds for neuters in all declensions: nominative and accusative are always identical.

sections.heading: Examples from Caesar and Cicero
sections.body:
templum magnum est. — The temple is large.
templum videō. — I see the temple.
mūrus templī altus est. — The wall of the temple is high.
bellum longum erat. — The war was long.
bella multa gessērunt. — They waged many wars.

Caesar writes: oppidum erat positum in colle. — The town was situated on a hill. 'oppidum' is nominative singular neuter, subject of 'erat'.

Cicero writes: dōnum deī. — The gift of a god. 'dōnum' is nominative/accusative neuter.

items.prompt: What is the nominative plural of bellum?
What is the accusative plural of templum?
Do neuter plural subjects take singular or plural verbs?
Name the two ways neuter nouns differ from masculine nouns of the second declension.
items.answer: 1. Nom. and acc. are identical. 2. Nom./acc. plural ends in -a.

words.gloss: The temple is in the forum.
The gifts of the gods are great.
